fact: A lone arsonist was caught inside the Reichstag after setting fire to it on the night of February 27, 1933
source: Marinus van der Lubbe was arrested at the scene; widely documented. See: "The Reichstag Fire" entry, United States Holocaust Memorial Museum

fact: President Hindenburg signed an emergency decree the morning after the fire, suspending civil liberties
source: The Decree of the Reich President for the Protection of People and State (Reichstag Fire Decree), signed February 28, 1933. Text available via German History in Documents and Images (GHDI), German Historical Institute

fact: The decree suspended constitutional protections including freedom of the press, freedom of speech, right to assembly, and protection against warrantless search and arrest without charge
source: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution and the Reichstag Fire Decree; detailed in "The Coming of the Third Reich" by Richard J. Evans (2003), Penguin Books

fact: The decree was drafted before the ashes cooled — implying it was prepared with extraordinary speed or possibly in advance
source: Historians have noted the decree's rapid drafting; discussed in "The Reichstag Fire" by Benjamin Carter Hett (2014), Oxford University Press. Hett examines evidence that emergency measures were already being contemplated before the fire.

fact: The fire gave Hitler emergency powers that were never rescinded, effectively ending democratic governance in Germany
source: The Reichstag Fire Decree remained in force throughout the Nazi regime (1933–1945). United States Holocaust Memorial Museum
